messages.mes:
The road took him down from the verge between fenced fields, ruts baked hard by dry weather, and joined a wider track where cart wheels had cut twin grooves over years. Ashbridge grew as he walked: first the wall, grey stone patched in places with paler, newer masonry, then the roofs behind it, then the gate itself—a double-arched opening with a timber frame, four spears leaning against the guardhouse wall, and a short line of farmers and carter's boys waiting to be waved through.

The gate guards barely looked up. One glanced at the staff slung across Alaric's back, then at the light robes beneath his traveling cloak, and turned away again with the flat attention of a man who had seen a hundred hedge mages come and go.

Inside, morning business was in full swing. A street of timber-fronted shops ran from the gate, a woman calling prices on hanging geese, a smith's hammer somewhere behind the buildings, the smell of coal smoke and horse dung and something sweet from a bakehouse. Two boys led a limping mule against the flow of traffic. Nobody gave the blond stranger a second look.

The Adventurers' Guild hall sat mid-street, marked by a carved shield above its door and a board outside papered with notices curling at the edges. Through the open door came lamplight, the smell of ale and wet leather, and the noise of a mid-morning crowd: a mixed group arguing over a map at a corner table, a woman in mail leaning on the counter, a clerk behind it sorting contract slips into a rack.

The clerk glanced up as Alaric came in, took in the staff and the robes, and gestured with her quill toward the counter's near end.

"New face? Registration's with me. If you're after work, the board's on the east wall."

"Alaric Red." The clerk said it back flatly, more to fix it in her head than to greet him, and pulled a ledger across the counter. The page she opened held two columns of names in a small, cramped hand. "Registration's two silver. One-time. That puts you on the rolls at Novice rank."

She dipped her quill and tapped a drop of ink back into the well.

"That's the Guild's rank—what work you're allowed to take. Novice means the low contracts: pest culls, deliveries, hedge-work. It climbs as you complete jobs. Separate thing from what you actually are." She gestured at his robes with the quill. "If you're a mage, the measuring stone will read your power rank when we do the intake. F through S. The Guild records it, but we don't grant it. You bring that with you or you don't."

Somewhere behind him a chair scraped and the group at the map table laughed at something.

"Two silver now, name in the book, then the stone, then you're free to take whatever the board will let you." She held the quill over the ledger and looked at him, waiting.

Two silver coins crossed the counter, and the clerk swept them into a drawer before writing his name into the ledger in the same cramped hand. "Alaric Red. Novice, as of today."

She came around the end of the counter and led him to a squat block of grey stone set on a plinth against the near wall, its surface worn smooth where countless hands had rested. "Palm flat, hold still. It just reads what you are—doesn't hurt."

The stone warmed faintly under his hand. A dull pulse of light moved through it, slow, and settled at a faint glow near the base of the block—low on its face, nowhere near the brighter bands higher up.

"F." The clerk noted it in the ledger without any particular inflection. "Common enough for a first reading. It climbs or it doesn't; the Guild just writes down what the stone says." She took a small stamped plate from a drawer behind the counter and slid it across to him—pale tin, the Guild's shield pressed into it, his name and Novice scratched beneath.

"That's yours. Show it at the desk when you take a contract, keep it on you when you work one. Lose it, and replacing it costs you another silver, so don't." She was already moving back to her rack of slips. "Board's on the east wall if you're after work."

He brought the slip to the counter, and the clerk took it, checked the shield stamp, and opened the ledger again. "Wagon Guard to the Quarry Gate. One Novice." She wrote his name beside the entry, pressed the Guild's stamp into the slip, and handed it back. "That's active as of now."

She pulled a stub of charcoal across a scrap of paper as she talked. "Client's Ossra Vane, paymistress for the stone quarry up the hills. Wagon leaves from the yard behind the Coinweight counting-house—south end of the market row, you'll see the strongbox cart and a driver named Pell. Payroll rides in the box; your job is that nobody takes it between here and the quarry gate."

"Waylayers have been watching the road, by her report. Nobody's hit the wagon yet, but they know the schedule now, which is why she's hiring. Could be nothing. Could be four hungry men with clubs. Novice contract, so likely the clubs." She slid the paper aside. "Pell knows the road. He's done this run six years. Listen to him if he says move."

Ashbridge's market row was still filling as he crossed it—stalls rolling up their shutters, a fishwife arguing with nobody in particular. At the south end he passed the Coinweight counting-house and its yard behind the fence, where a heavy cart stood with a tarp over its box and a broad man in a leather apron checking the wheels. Pell, most like, waiting on his guard. Alaric kept walking.

The Quarry Road climbed west out of the city gate, a rutted track of packed mud and broken stone winding up through scrub hills. Carts had worn twin grooves into it deep enough to catch an ankle. The morning was cool, the wind smelling of cut stone and nothing greener. Twice he passed loads coming down—a mule train with saddle-baskets of rough-hewn blocks, then a single carter who gave him a nod and a once-over and nothing more.

It took the better part of two hours. The quarry gate showed itself before the quarry did: a timber palisade across the road where the hills pinched narrow, a watch platform at one end, smoke rising beyond it. A pair of guards in quarry grey leaned on the barrier, and the nearer one straightened as Alaric came up the last stretch.

"You're walking light for this road," the guard said. "That'd make you the Guild's man, or a very lost pilgrim." He squinted at the staff. "Guild's man, then. Only the pay wagon's not due till midday—Pell holds it till the sun's high, that's his habit. Vane will want to know why you've come up ahead of it instead of riding with it." He jerked a thumb at a gap in the palisade. "She's in the tally shed. Or you can wait here at the gate, if you'd rather watch the road. Road's the direction the trouble comes from, mind."

The guard shrugged and went back to his leaning. "Your funeral's your own. There's a stool."

Alaric took up a spot by the palisade where the road showed itself for a good stretch below—scrub hills folding around it, the ruts catching what light the morning gave. The guards traded talk about a cracked millstone and somebody's sister, and mostly ignored him. An hour passed. Smoke shifted with the wind. A goat wandered up and was shooed off.

The wagon came into view a little before midday, one mule, tarped box, Pell walking beside it with a cudgel hooked through his belt. Alaric had watched the road long enough to notice the second thing first: two men a few hundred paces back of the wagon, keeping its pace, keeping the distance. Not walking like carters or quarry men. One had a long coat despite the climb, and they stayed wide of the ruts, along the scrub edge where the ground was softer to cross but harder to watch.

Pell saw the gate and raised a hand. He hadn't looked back—or if he had, it hadn't shown.

The guard on the platform called down, "Wagon's in sight. And two behind it, if my eyes still work."

"Every payroll day there's two behind it," the nearer guard said, though he'd pushed off the palisade and was standing straight now, hand resting easy near his hip. "Most days they're quarry men off shift. Those two aren't walking like quarry men."

The wagon drew closer, gravel under the wheels, the mule's ears twitching. Pell was near enough now to hail. The two figures behind held their distance at the last bend, out of easy shouting range, and stopped there, as if content to watch the wagon reach the gate.

The wagon's ruts still held the morning's prints, and the last bend sat empty by the time Alaric passed it—no long coats, no watchers, only scrub and wind. She counted out coins onto the counter, fourteen coppers stacked in short rows. "One hundred forty copper for the Wagon Guard, Guild payout, paid in full."

messages.mes:
Chandler's Row smelled of tallow and dried yarrow, the physickers' hall a squat stone building with a low doorway and bundles of herbs hanging under its eaves. A boy was sweeping the step out front and gave Alaric a look on his way in.

Inside, the air was warm and sharp with spirits. A woman in a grey apron was grinding something in a mortar behind the counter, sleeves rolled to the elbow, forearms freckled and strong.

"If you're bleeding, sit and wait," she said without looking up. "If you're not bleeding, say what you want."

She glanced up then, took in the staff on his back and the Guild plate at his belt, and set the pestle down. "Ah. The tonic run." She wiped her hands on her apron. "Sister Maren. You're quicker than I expected—good. The wardens have been biting their nails over it."

She went through to the back and returned with a crate the size of a bread box, wooden, roped at the corners, a blob of green wax stamped with her seal spread across the lid seam. She set it on the counter and looked at him, weighing more than the crate. "It's a half-day's walk to the Wayshrine. The crate's not heavy, but it doesn't like being dropped, and the seal doesn't like being broken. Wardens sign for it where the paper says." She held it out. "Take it to them, and mind the last stretch of road—the weirs' side, past the standing stone. Folk have been seeing something on it at dusk."

messages.mes:
The crate went into the crook of his arm, light enough but awkward, the rope handles biting his fingers after the first stretch. Maren watched him out the door and went back to her mortar.

Ashbridge's west gate took a copper of toll and a bored wave from the wall men. Beyond it the road ran straight through hedged farmland, cart ruts baked hard by the sun, a woman driving geese who shuffled off the road without a glance at him. An hour on, the hedges gave way to reed ground, and the smell of the flats came up—mud, cut reeds, standing water. The eel-weirs showed far off to the left, a lattice of stakes in the shallows.

The road bent toward a standing stone at the third hour, a leaning grey slab furred with lichen where the wayshrine road forked off toward low hills. The sun was getting low and orange by then, and the light lay long across the reeds.

He saw it before he reached the stone. Across the road, in the soft mud of a drainage ditch, a line of tracks crossed from the reed side to the hill side—three-toed, clawed, each print longer than his hand, spaced wide. Whatever made them had been heavy. The mud in the deepest print still glistened, edges not yet crusted. Fresh, or near it. The tracks went up the slope and into the bracken, toward the wayshrine road.

The standing stone stood maybe forty paces on. Beyond it, a mile of open road to the shrine, where a palisade and a watch-fire smoke were just visible against the hills.

The reeds to the left rustled once—wind, or not—and went still. The crate sat in his arm, sealed and roped, and the sun kept sinking.

messages.mes:
Past the standing stone the hedges were gone and the road lay open between reed flats and the rising ground, the palisade a dark line ahead with the smoke standing straight above it in the still air. The crate rode in the crook of his arm, and the light went from orange to grey-blue at the edges.

Halfway along that last stretch, the reeds to the left went quiet in a way the rest of the flats did not. No frogs, no wind-shift. Then a sound carried across the water—something big drinking, a slow lapping, and the knock of a stake as a body brushed past one of the weirs.

It came out of the reeds forty yards back the way he'd come. Long, low, taller than a man at the shoulder hump, scaled a dull reed-green, its tail dragging a furrow through the mud of the roadside. A heavy three-toed head swung toward the road and stopped there, nostrils working. Its eyes were small and yellow, and they fixed on the shape standing in its path with a crate in its arms.

It didn't charge. It lowered its head a little and took one heavy step onto the road, claws sinking into the ruts, then another, cutting off the way back to Ashbridge. Ahead, the wayshrine palisade was still a mile off—a torch had been lit on one of the wall posts, tiny against the hills. Whether anyone there could see a man and a beast on the road in the failing light was another matter.

The creature stood in the middle of the road, tail swaying slow, watching him.

The ditch offered him little. He went along the bank in the last light and looked the carcass over, and the hide told the story plainly enough: the scales were thick as a thumb and fitted tight as roof tiles, the burned patches split and stinking, and beneath them the flesh was dense and dark. He had no blade meant for skinning, no hands free besides the one holding the crate, and no clear notion of what part of such a thing anyone would want. He prodded a foreleg, tipped the heavy three-toed foot with the staff, found nothing loose, nothing worn, nothing carried. The mouth held nothing but worn teeth. Whatever value the beast had would need a wagon, a block and tackle and men who knew the trade, and none of that was here. He left it wedged in the mud for the swamp to keep and climbed back to the road.

The mile went by in full dark. Frogs ran along the ditches beside him the whole way, and twice something small broke cover ahead and crossed in the black between the reed beds. The crate rode steady in the crook of his arm, rope and green wax seal whole. When the wayshrine's torch finally swung into view it was a small orange point on a wall post, and then the building came with it—a long low stone hall with a palisade yard, a fenced garden patch, and lamplight in two windows. A dog started barking from behind the fence before he was within fifty yards, a deep working bark, and a light moved inside the hall. By the time he reached the torch post the yard gate was opening and a broad man in a road warden's leather coat stood in it with a lantern held high and a spear leaned against the gatepost.

"Stop there," the man called, unhurried but firm, the dog pressing his legs. "Who's on the road?"

He set the crate on the bench and stepped back, and the warden came to it with the lantern low. The second warden had come out of the hall by then—an older woman with a wool shawl and a healer's plain apron underneath her coat—and she stood at his shoulder while he worked the rope.

"Green wax, physickers' mark," she said, before he'd even tilted it to the light. "That's Maren's stamp."

The warden turned the crate twice, ran his thumb around the wax, and grunted. "Whole. No cracks, no water in the rope." He lifted one end, testing the weight, then set it down again. "That's the lot, then. Nine vials of fever tonic, sealed and sound." He straightened and looked at Alaric with a different expression than at the gate—not warm exactly, but settled. "You walked that road in the dark, past a dead marsh-drake, with this under your arm. Sister Maren'll hear it went well."

The woman was already taking the crate up in both arms, easy with the weight. "The fever's in three households past the ford," she said, mostly to the warden. "This is the first of it to arrive." She carried it into the hall, and the lamplight took her and it.

The warden leaned the spear back against the wall and nodded at the fire pit. "You've earned a warm patch of ground tonight if you want it, or there's hay under the overhang that's drier. Either way you're welcome till morning—the road's no kinder in the dark than it was an hour ago."

The warden took it without offence. "Suit yourself. Torch burns all night on the post if the road brings you back." He walked him as far as the gate, and the dog followed at his heel, and then the yard light fell away behind and the road was dark again.

The mile to the drake was slower going than coming. Alaric gave the ditch a wide berth where the thing lay—its smell reached him before the shape did—and the frogs went quiet around that stretch and started again past it. After that the road climbed out of the reed beds and the air dried, and the walk became ordinary: ruts underfoot, wind in the hedges, far off a light in a farmhouse window that came and went behind trees.

Ashbridge showed itself first as a dull glow above the hedgerows, then the wall, then the gate towers with their lanterns. The gate watch was two men and a brazier; one glanced at his guild slip when he offered it, waved the other back to the fire, and jerked his thumb through. "Late one," the man said, without much interest. "Gate shuts at midnight if you're going out again."

Inside, the streets were quiet but not empty. A tavern near the gate still had light and noise spilling from its shutters, the smell of ale and roast onions reaching the road. Further in, the lanes were lamplit at the corners and empty between, and the Guild hall stood dark except for one window on the ground floor, where a clerk was still at work over papers by candlelight.

The pits went deeper than they'd looked from the road — three cuts, then a fourth behind a shoulder of earth, all of them flooded to varying degrees, the far banks torn up worse than the near one. The center of the sink rose.

Mud came first, sheeting off a skull-wide head in ropes, and then the head itself, grey-brown like the others but broad as a door, eyes set forward and small, nostrils flaring wide over the water. The tongue came back in. The head tilted, one small eye fixing on him, and the wyrm's throat swelled — the skin there stretching and paling, a lump traveling up it the way water travels in a drainpipe, gathering.

Down across the cuts, both voices at the sheds had gone quiet.

messages.mes:
The market district lay north of the Guild, down streets that narrowed and grew louder — awnings, barrows, the smell of fish and hot bread, a smith's hammer somewhere behind the shuttered fronts. Alaric worked through it with his pack heavy on his shoulders and the venom sacs wrapped stiff against his back.

He asked after a broker at a fish stall and got a shrug. A chandler pointed him toward a shopfront with a painted sign of a boar's head and antlers, which looked promising until he stood in its doorway and found it sold sausage, cheese and smoked hams — a pie shop with hunting pretensions, the boar a menu, not a trophy. The woman behind the counter looked at his mud-caked clothes and offered him a meat pie at a copper.

Past that, the morning went on the same way. The cloth row, the coppersmiths, a leatherworker who handled one of the skin plates, turned it over twice and handed it back — good hide, she said, but she tanned, she didn't buy, and who'd brought it in was a tallow-boiler's question, not hers. A carter loading cabbages thought there might be a man who bought such things near the shambles, or possibly it was his brother did that, he wasn't sure which.

By the time the church bells rang the hour the sun had climbed past the rooftops and the pack straps had worn grooves in his shoulders. The monster parts rode where they'd started, unsold. Down an alley mouth off the cloth row a painted board hung crooked over a door: a crossed knife and shears, the letters half-flaked. It was not obviously a shop for anything.

messages.mes:
The door stuck, then gave. Inside was one long room, low-ceilinged, dim, and smelled of salt, tanning oil and something older underneath — a sharp animal reek that never quite left a room where monsters came apart. Bundles hung from the beams: dried fins, a shed snakeskin long as a rowboat, something feathered and grey wrapped in cloth. A counter of split planks ran down the left side, and behind it a small woman with grey-streaked hair and a leather apron was scoring lines along a stretched hide with a curved knife. She finished her cut before she looked up.

"Door's open, so you're either selling or lost." Her eyes went to the pack, then to the mud on him, and stayed there a moment. "That's not bread you're carrying. I can smell it from here. Take it off and put it on the counter."

She set the knife down and wiped her hands on the apron, waiting.

messages.mes:
The pack thumped onto the counter and Alaric unbuckled it. He laid the pieces out one by one on the split planks: the flat grey-brown skin plates, still stiff with clay at the edges; a fang the length of his hand, curved like a hook; the venom sacs wrapped in cloth, leaking a faint smell that made the shopkeeper's nostrils tighten; and the heavier plate, the broad one, slicked flat and rough as a curbstone.

She came around the counter without hurrying. Her hands moved over each piece in turn — thumbnail pressed into a skin plate to test the grain, the fang turned to the light and run under her thumb along the root, the venom sac held up and gently squeezed while she watched the color of what beaded at the puncture. The big plate she weighed in both arms, then dropped on the counter with a knock that shook the hanging bundles.

"Three wyrms' worth, by the look of it. Clay pits?" She didn't wait for an answer. "Hide's been cut rough and there's pit-mud worked into two of these plates, but the grain's sound. Fang's whole, root uncracked — that's worth more than most bring me, they snap them prying." She pinched the venom sac again, sniffed her fingers, and set it down with a little more care than the rest. "Sacs are intact. That's the money piece."

She wiped her hands and looked at him properly for the first time.

"Eight silver for the lot. Six for the hides and fang, two for the sacs. Before you huff at me — a rendering yard gives you three and boils them for tallow. I dress, salt and resell. Eight is fair and it's in coin today." She folded her arms over the apron. "Or you take the sacs back and try an alchemist, if you fancy waiting a week and being talked down to."

messages.mes:
"Done, then." She unfolded her arms and got to work, and her hands showed she'd done it a thousand times. The skin plates went into a wicker basket lined with salt. The fang wrapped in rag. The venom sacs she carried to a small stone jar in the back shelf and settled each into it with tongs, gentle as eggs, before she came back wiping her palms.

The pieces Alaric had carried out of the clay pits were gone off the counter inside a few minutes. In their place she counted coins out of a locked drawer under the counter — silver pieces, one by one onto the wood where he could see them, eight in a short row. She slid the row across with one finger.

"There. And you'll not get better on the sacs elsewhere, so don't bother trying." She pulled the basket toward her and was already reaching for the curved knife again. "If you go back to those pits and bring me more in that shape, same price. Whole roots, unbroken sacs. Come asking for Marta."

The bell over the door hung silent behind him whenever he chose to use it, the midday market still loud in the street outside, the eight silver warm in his pouch alongside the Guild plate and the contract slips.
